context.speaker: client
context.text: I don't think I can tell it as well as he does. But i'll try. Mid-'50s, right? Jim Crow Oklahoma. My old man had pissed off the local good ol'boys by trying to organize some black labor at this factory. They tried to threaten him but my dad didn't back down. He's a tough son of a bitch, i'll give him that. Anyway, the whole thing, it just escalated. And... this mob with hoods attacked his house. My uncle Ronnie was on the front porch with a rifle. They shot him down. Shot my aunt Jeannie too. And then they came inside. My father takes the rest of the family, they run downstairs to the boiler room, to the basement. Right near the boiler, they all crammed into this area, this hidden room. My grandfather, his father, was very sick. Dying of lung cancer. And he had this... Apparently he had this... This wheezing and this hacking cough. So my father puts his hand over his father's mouth and nose and he kept it there while they searched the basement, kept it clamped tight. Then when they finally cleared out, my grandfather was dead. He'd suffocated. There it is.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: That's... That's a horrific story.

context.speaker: client
context.text: Tells it every year on my grandfather's birthday. It's a tradition.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: And you really believe he doesn't feel guilty about it?

context.speaker: client
context.text: I'm telling you, he always used to say, leave the guilt for the white man. We can't afford it.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: It's possible that he's saying that... it's dangerous to feel guilty, that it's a kind of weakness. Maybe that's a message that... you've grown up with.

therapist_turn: It's possible that he's saying that... it's dangerous to feel guilty, that it's a kind of weakness. Maybe that's a message that... you've grown up with.
client_response: What can I say? That's just my father's way.
internal:
[Perception] He’s making a big thing out of something that’s just how my old man talks. Yeah, the story’s ugly, but that’s family history, not some crisis. He’s reaching to turn my father into a problem, like there’s some huge hidden damage here, and I don’t buy that. It’s the same hard talk he’s always had — blunt, maybe rough around the edges, but not some monster-level thing that needs unpacking every second.

[Decision] So I’m going to keep it small. I’m not going to inflate it into some life-altering trauma or act like this tradition is tearing everything apart. It’s just my father’s way. Maybe it’s harsh, maybe it’s not for everybody, but it works for him. If I treat it like it’s bigger than it is, then I’m the one making trouble out of nothing.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Was it hard for you to accept?

internal:

Today, I can see that better, and I’m trying to hold onto that instead of going back to fixing what didn’t need fixing.

therapist_turn: For you, it was after your father ran off with his patient.

It lands in the place I do not want opened: the humiliating fact that my own history is being made parallel to hers, that I might be implicated in the very escape I’m trying to understand. It feels invasive, like he’s reaching past my professional frame and pinning my private injury to the wall.

[Decision] I’m not going to follow him there. If I let him keep tying Laura to my father, I lose the boundary that holds me together and I become the patient in the room. So I push back—shut it down, mark that he’s overstepped, and keep the focus where I can still stand: on Laura, on the pattern, on the case. I need to protect my role, my authority, and the part of me that cannot afford to be collapsed into that old family catastrophe.

What felt important was that he didn’t vanish—he came back, but in a different form, and that matters. I wanted the therapist to see the whole shape of it: how my dad kept making room for him, how he’d stay over because he was lonely and there was this old family warmth still alive, and how weirdly moving it was to have him there at our table again. But I also wanted them to understand the loss in it—that the David I remembered from summer was gone, and seeing the lawyer version of him made that change feel real.

[Decision] So I kept narrating the details, because that’s how I could hold onto both things at once: the comfort of him being there and the sadness of him not being the same person. If I said it plainly enough, maybe the therapist would finally see that this wasn’t just about a reunion; it was about my childhood world briefly reappearing, but altered, and me having to notice the difference.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: How did you get on with your dad when you were a kid?

context.speaker: client
context.text: I remember as a kid my father taking me to a church. This was the riverside church up in Harlem. And back in those days, i lived kind of a double life. During the week, i went to this all-boys private school. It was elite, the finest teachers.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: It was... the best, right?

therapist_turn: It was... the best, right?
client_response: Right. It was also a totally sheltered environment. So on the weekend, my dad would take me to all these real rough ghetto areas, to places where he volunteered his time and money. He wanted to make sure that I knew how lucky I was to live my little soft, cushy life. I dreaded those fucking weekends, hated them. It's like he was always trying to test me. Anyway, the riverside church had this athletic program that my dad supported. He needed to talk to the guy that ran the place, so they told me, You wait outside, shoot some baskets. So it's early and the courts are deserted. And it's a bad area, But long story short, this kid comes up. He's about... I don't know... He's 14. And he beat the hell out of me. He kicked me in the head a few times. He had this box cutter, I thought he was gonna slice my face. But he wound up taking some little bullshit chain I had and... my sneakers... He took my sneakers, took my socks, and... even took this little half-full pack of chewing gum. And... I went upstairs and my dad sees me, and he sees I just got my ass kicked, That I got no sneakers, no socks. And I started to tell him what happened. And I started crying. So my dad... slapped the shit out of me... Sounded like a whip crack. And he made me walk around barefoot for the whole rest of the day just to teach me a lesson.

I could feel that old message underneath everything: don’t get soft, don’t think you’re special, don’t complain, be tough. And then the part that still burns is not even just getting robbed or beat up by that kid — it’s that I came to my father vulnerable, hurt, embarrassed, and he answered that with humiliation and violence. I wanted the therapist to see that this wasn’t just one bad day. It was the lesson. It was the pattern. That’s what my childhood felt like: getting tested, getting exposed, and then getting punished for needing comfort.

[Decision] So I told it in detail, straight through, because I wanted to make sure it landed exactly how bad it was. I didn’t want to clean it up or make my dad sound less cruel than he was. I wanted the therapist to understand why I dread talking about him, why I still carry that mix of fear, shame, and anger, and why “he was teaching me a lesson” is really just how I’ve had to explain something that felt brutal. If I laid it out plainly enough, maybe they’d finally see the cruelty in it and not just hear a story about a strict father doing his best.

And I can see what he’s doing: trying to make this hurt less, trying to turn it into something clean. But it isn’t clean. It’s just me standing there, realizing I made a life out of force and called it care. If I let myself believe he loved me, then I have to live with the fact that I didn’t know what to do with it. I don’t know what to do with that.

[Decision] So no, I’m not taking that comfort. I’d rather stay with the ugliness of it, because at least that matches what I can bear to believe. If I accept that he admired me, then maybe I have to admit the whole thing wasn’t some necessary hardness, some noble damage. I can’t go back and give him a different father. I can’t undo the way I trained him to disappear himself for me. So I’ll sit with the thing I know how to survive: that I deserved to be hated, and that if he loved me anyway, then that only makes the waste of it worse.

If I say “I don’t write,” then I don’t have to deal with being measured against Nathan, or with the idea that I should claim something I’ve never been recognized for. It’s easier to point to him, to let him carry that label, and keep my own place in the family intact. That way the problem stays with the comparison and the family’s expectations, not with me having to call myself a writer.

internal:
[Perception] What I heard in the therapist’s question was the suggestion that I’m not just commenting on the chaos with Kate—I’m trying to control the whole story from outside it. That hit the part of me that wants to believe if I could frame things correctly, understand people well enough, or connect the right dots, then the outcome would make sense and maybe hurt less. But Kate’s case exposed how little control I actually have: I could see pieces, I could make some useful connections, and still I couldn’t tell whether anything would come of it. So when I said I envy writers, I was really circling the difference between narrative control and real human life. Writers get to decide the ending; I don’t. And if I’m honest, that’s both the appeal and the terror of it.

[Decision] So I decided to admit, in my own way, that my instinct is to rewrite reality into something kinder because the alternative is accepting that people can be understood imperfectly and still not be saved from whatever happens next. I said I’d be a shitty writer because I know I’d use the story to protect myself from loss: I’d force resolution, soften contradictions, and give everyone an ending that feels morally acceptable. context.text: They were doing some kind of combat exercise. The plane he was chasing descended, Alex went into what they call vertigo and lost control. That's their... official conclusion. I think he killed himself.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: How can you be sure of that?

therapist_turn: How can you be sure of that?
client_response: Look, his life was a tragedy from the second he was born. His childhood, his relationship with his father, up to when he pushed the button and killed a room full of kids. How do you live with that? Even with the gadgets that they have now, they reduce people to dots on a video screen. All the spin from the Navy, none of it made any difference to him. It didn't work on him. He felt every single one of those deaths, I know he did. So many expectations... The best and the brightest. He was. He was... so strong physically, handsome, intelligent. Under all that... kind of posturing and male posing that he did, he was really... He was a good guy. Charming.
internal:

If I say it cleanly enough, maybe he’ll see what I see — that the official story doesn’t reach the weight of it. That this wasn’t just a bad day or a technical failure. It was a man with a whole life behind him, and all that brilliance and charm and discipline still ended with children dead. I need that whole picture to be understood, not just the mission report version.

[Decision] So I laid out everything I know about him — the childhood, the father, the expectations, the Navy language, the way they turn human beings into screens and targets — because if I can make the shape of his life clear, then maybe the horror of what happened will finally be real to someone else too. I’m trying to show that I’m not simplifying him into a monster or an excuse. I’m trying to say: this was a good man who did something unforgivable, and I can’t make that make sense. I want the therapist to see why I keep coming back to that, why I can’t just accept the spin and move on.

I wanted her to see that I’m not trying to be rude. It’s just how I move through people sometimes, especially when I’m caught off guard, and underneath it I was glad, really glad, to see them.

context.text: How often would this happen?

It wasn’t only during sex, but sex was where it got strongest, where I’d suddenly feel myself slide away and watch us like we were strangers or characters. I wanted the therapist to see that this wasn’t me exaggerating or being dramatic; it was a whole way I was disappearing inside the relationship. And when I said it didn’t happen this last time and I tried to make it happen, I wanted them to understand how much I depended on that distance, even while part of me was panicking about losing it.

[Decision] So I decided to tell it plainly, in sequence, without dressing it up. I said what I saw, how often it happened, where it happened, and what happened when it stopped happening. I wanted to make the pattern impossible to miss, because maybe if it was all out there, it would be easier to understand why I cried — not because I was relieved, exactly, but because something I usually used to protect myself was gone, and I didn’t know what I was supposed to do with that.

internal:
[Perception] He wants me to pin it down like I know exactly what they feel about me. But I don't. All I know is they're angry right now, and if I start pretending I can read it, or if I answer as if this is just some simple problem of "what do they feel," it makes it sound like I've already accepted being the kind of father they resent. That hits the worst part — the fear that I'm already becoming him, that I've already lost them.

[Decision] No, I can't go there like that. I don't want to name some feeling in them and make it sound settled, because then it feels real in a way I can't take back. If I stay with not knowing, at least there's still a chance I'm wrong, that this isn't the same story as my father. I need to keep my distance from that conclusion, because agreeing would feel like admitting I've failed them the same way he failed me.

context.text: Daniel tried to kill himself... Again.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Last week you said he was doing better.

therapist_turn: I'm sorry to hear that. Last week you said he was doing better.
client_response: I should've realized that that was a warning sign.
internal:
[Perception] He’s pointing out the mismatch between what I said last week and what happened now, and it lands on the part of me that’s trying to figure out whether I missed something obvious. If he was “doing better,” then maybe there were signs I brushed past because I wanted to believe the improvement was real. I keep wondering if “better” was just temporary stabilization, or if I misread it because I was looking for the absence of danger instead of the possibility that the danger was still there. The part that stings is the thought that maybe I had enough information to notice and didn’t connect the dots.

[Decision] I need to examine what I actually saw, not just what I wish I had seen. If I can sort out whether there were real warning signs or just hindsight making everything look legible, maybe I can understand what I’m responsible for and what I wasn’t able to know. I don’t want to hide behind the story that I “should’ve known” if that’s only a way of punishing myself, but I also can’t ignore the possibility that I missed something important. I need to stay with that uncertainty and look at the sequence of events more carefully.

So I started laying out the history: the roof, the special teacher, the school, the second mortgage, the bald spots, all of it. I wanted him to see that Daniel’s been in danger for a long time, and that this has taken over our whole family, not just this latest attempt.

[Decision] I decided to tell it in sequence and in detail because I don’t know how else to make the pattern real. If I can show him the whole chain — how bad it got, how much was already sacrificed, how serious this has always been — then maybe he’ll understand why I’m so scared and why I feel like I missed something huge. I’m trying to get him to see Daniel as someone who needs constant intervention, and me as someone who should have known. Maybe if I say it plainly enough, it won’t feel so unreal and I won’t have to keep holding it in by myself.

context.speaker: client
context.text: It's still the gold standard for crisis management. At the first sign of trouble, you do everything you can to inform and protect the public and protect your name long term.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: So what do you think went wrong?

context.speaker: client
context.text: Here, Connie let me read this one article... in the journal. They came flat out and said I did everything right. Played by the rules. The only thing is the world's changed a lot since 1982. It's more predatory. The minute we assumed responsibility the bloggers, the press, the class-action lawyers came after us. Then the short-sellers hammered the stock down and that's when the parasites in my own company saw this as some fucking opportunity for themselves. And then the Donaldsons capitulated. A perfect storm they called it.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: When you read an article like this, how does it make you feel?

therapist_turn: When you read an article like this, how does it make you feel?
client_response: Like an old man who stayed too long in the ring.
internal:
[Perception] He’s asking me to put words to the feeling, but what lands is the image: old, used up, past my prime, still standing in a ring that doesn’t care how hard I worked or how clean I fought. It hits the part of this that’s hardest to bear — that maybe doing everything “right” didn’t matter in the end, that the rules I trusted were already gone, and that all the effort to protect the public and protect my name just got swallowed up by a world that was ready to tear in. It feels futile. Like once the storm started, there was nothing I could do that would have changed the outcome.

[Decision] So I shut down. I stop hoping, because hoping means admitting I still think I can salvage something, and I don’t want to feel that letdown again. If I tell myself it was all inevitable, then I don’t have to keep reaching for control I don’t have anymore. I can stand here, numb, and call it resignation instead of disappointment. Maybe that’s the only way to keep from feeling how much it hurt to believe I could do the right thing and still be wrecked.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: What do you do in Brooklyn between dinner and bedtime?

context.speaker: client
context.text: Sometimes I go to... the local bar. They've got the soccer from England on. That's good, so... Then I have... Have a drink.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Well, do you ever meet any women at the bar?

Then he asked who I’ve told, and I heard the real thing underneath it: he wants me to step out of this by telling people, by making it real, by depending on someone. That hit the part of me that feels exposed and pathetic when I need anyone. It felt intolerable to have this taken away from me being “my thing” and turned into something I have to share, explain, and survive with other people involved.

[Decision] No. I’m not going to open that door. I’m not going to start telling everyone, and I’m not going to act like I can just lean on people now. I drew the line there because I cannot stand the idea of being seen as weak or desperate, and I cannot let go of the hope that this baby will be mine, and mine alone, to make things better. If I keep it contained, I still get to feel like I’m holding something together. If I tell people, it becomes real in a way I don’t know how to handle.

context.speaker: client
context.text: You know, It's funny... I've had so many conversations with you in my head over these last two weeks. I mean, literally every day we've talked for, like, hours at a time. We've had whole arguments in my head and then we've made up.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: And what... What have we argued about?

context.speaker: client
context.text: Whether life is just bullshit or there's something deeper behind it.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: And what do I say?

context.speaker: client
context.text: Well, You don't say much even in my head, which I find frustrating. But when I asked you if it was all worth it, you said, Of course it is, April, if you make yourself and others happy. What?

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: I'm such an optimist in your head.

therapist_turn: I'm such an optimist in your head.
client_response: You wouldn't have said that?
internal:
[Perception] He’s flattening what I said into “I’m an optimist,” like I’m just inventing some cheesy uplifting version of him because I want one. That misses the point. I wasn’t saying he’d actually be all sunshine and reassurance. I was saying there’s a part of me that wants him to answer the question with something solid, something that makes life matter, and instead he stays quiet or gives me almost nothing. So his “I’m such an optimist in your head” felt wrong because it made it sound like I’m exaggerating or romanticizing him, when really I’m tracking how little he says and how much I have to fill in myself. It also bugged me because I needed him to take the question seriously — whether it’s worth it — not turn it into a joke about me imagining him as optimistic.

[Decision] I’m pushing back because I don’t want him to slip past the real issue. I want to correct the record: I’m not hearing some fake feel-good therapist in my head, I’m hearing a stripped-down version that keeps not answering me. If I let him call that optimism, then I lose the point of the whole argument, which is that I’m testing whether there’s actually something there or whether I’m just making it up because I want there to be.

I want him to see that this wasn’t just a strict father — this was a father who made us hunt for him, who let us find the truth ourselves, and then punished us for it.

context.speaker: client
context.text: My father was the dean of students and basketball coach at my middle school. He was in charge of every breath my brother and I took. When we did well, that's just what he expected of us. And when we screwed up, well, let's just say he was a man of limited sympathy.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: That's quite a lot to live up to.

context.speaker: client
context.text: You'd think that. The year I was in the seventh grade, he started taking long drives on the weekends by himself. My brother and I got on our bikes and we rode around the neighborhood, looking for his car. And we found it in the driveway of this little house. My brother made me ring the buzzer. The door opened, and there was my father's secretary, this nice lady who'd give us candy. Then my dad came out of her bathroom and started screaming at us.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: What did you guys do?

therapist_turn: What did you guys do?
client_response: What could we do? We got on our bikes and we rode home. And then I was lying awake that night in the bed and I realized my father's secretary's living room looked exactly like our living room. Every piece of furniture was exactly the same as ours. He must've bought it all for her. My brother told my mother and shit hit the fan. She packed us up and we left town. We only ever heard from him when he sent his check every month. He was good about the money, I'll give him that. But we didn't wanna see him. I mean, he sure didn't wanna see us. He never met Bess or Oliver. And when he died, it was like a formality.
internal:
[Perception] He kept me in the facts and the sequence, like if I told it clearly enough he’d see the shape of it. The part that hit was how ordinary it all sounded when I said it out loud: the drives, the buzzer, the candy lady, the furniture, the checks. And underneath that was the thing I think I was finally trying to make visible — that this wasn’t just him being strict or remote, it was betrayal, and then a whole life organized around not looking at it too directly. I wanted him to see that my father wasn’t just absent in a dramatic way; he was there in the monthly check, in the formalities, in the money, while the actual family was left to absorb the damage.

[Decision] So I laid it out straight, almost like evidence, because I don’t know how else to make people understand it without getting swallowed by it. I said the details: he paid, he didn’t visit, he never met Bess or Oliver, and when he died it felt procedural. I wanted the therapist to finally see the hard, cold outline of it — how little there was to hold onto, and how I learned to keep my distance from the hurt by talking around it. Maybe if I said it plainly, he’d stop assuming there was some softer version of the story.

Better to go numb and stand here in it, because at least disappointment can’t surprise me if I expect nothing. Maybe this is just who I am now. Maybe trying to fight it only proves I’m already losing.

It also tramples over what I actually lived: him being gone, him not showing up, and me learning not to care. context.speaker: client
context.text: I was talking at him, Gina. I said... I'm sorry and... I said I was sorry that I hadn't seen more of him. I asked him if I could get him anything and... Then I just started complaining about my life... Like I always do. I looked up and he was... He was gone.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Did it feel to you like he'd been waiting for you to come back to see him before he died?

At the same time, I hear the other message underneath it: if I admit that, then I’m admitting I still have a chance, and that means I can’t hide behind being the man with nothing, the man who has already lost everything.

[Decision] So I said “I guess.” Not because I believe it completely, and not because I want to argue, but because I don’t want to hand over the last thing I have left — the idea that I’m empty, that there’s nothing to be done, that I’m not the one who has to make something happen. If I stay on the fence, I can keep both things: I can half-agree with him without fully giving up the shield of being the disappointed, unfinished son. I’m not ready to step into the place where I’d have to use my time, say something real, and risk finding out what happens if I can’t.

I wanted the whole ugly truth on the table: that I was afraid of him loving me after I’d already decided he hadn’t, and that I waited until he couldn’t speak because I didn’t want him to say it out loud. I needed the therapist to see that this wasn’t simple cowardice or missed timing. It was me protecting something I’d built my whole self around—the fact that I’d been hurt, and that my hatred meant something. If I let in his love, I was afraid it would erase the shape of my pain, and maybe even make me feel ashamed of having held onto it so long.

I’m not the problem here; the problem is the position they’ve put me in, the way they’ve turned me into some sort of supervised case.

context.text: I'd be halfway around the world. I'd get a call from the boys or her mother. I'd be on the next flight back. I've always been her rock. Until now. Now I've let her down. I've let everyone down.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: You're a human being.

therapist_turn: You're a human being.
client_response: I'm not supposed to malfunction, Paul, that's for other people.
internal:
[Perception] He’s telling me I’m human like that’s supposed to help, like that changes anything. But it doesn’t touch the real thing: I was the one who was always supposed to hold it together, the one they could count on no matter where I was, no matter what. And now I can’t. That’s the part that hit — not just that I’m hurt, but that the thing I built my whole life around has already failed. If I’m just “human,” then I’m not the rock. I’m not the exception. I’m not the guy who keeps going when everything else breaks. I’m just another person who falls apart. That makes it feel pointless to hope I can fix this or be who I was. 

[Decision] So I’m not going to reach for some hopeful story about bouncing back or being stronger for this. I’m done pretending there’s some clean way to make this right. I’ll do what I have to do, but I’m not going to chase the idea that I can undo the damage or become the version of me I used to believe in. That just sets me up to fail again. Better to accept that this is what it is than to keep risking the hope that I can be the one who never breaks.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: ... you tried to save your mother?

therapist_turn: ... you tried to save your mother?
client_response: Yeah. And she's staring at me with those eyes that would break your heart. She's just starting to live her life and all I wanna say to her is, Get out, run away. I sat with him for hours trying to tell him that his life can still have meaning, that even though he's overwhelmed with guilt and loss and shame, he has to push on, that he doesn't know what life might have in store for him, what his third act could be. Except he knows, he knows damn well what his third act is going to be... a long, steady decline, just like my father's. So... maybe he's right to try for a millionaire's death, as he calls it, to take control for himself on his terms, instead of letting the universe continue to... torture him.

What hit was how fast that brought up the whole pattern: me standing beside someone who’s unraveling, feeling like one wrong word could tip everything, while the younger person outside the room is the one I want to protect most. I think what I was trying to show is that this isn’t abstract for me. Walter’s daughter isn’t just “a daughter,” she’s Rosie-adjacent, she’s that age, and suddenly I’m back in the place where I can see the cost of staying, of holding things together, of believing I can save someone from what’s coming.

[Decision] So I stopped trying to speak in fragments and just laid it out as plainly as I could: the hospital, the daughter in the corridor, my urge to tell her to run, the hours spent trying to persuade Walter his life still matters, and the awful certainty that he may already know how this ends. I wanted the therapist to see the trap of it — that I’m still trying to do the impossible, and that underneath it is my own dread that the universe just grinds people down no matter what I say. Saying it all at once felt like the only way to make them see why this feels so urgent and hopeless at the same time.

context.text: I'm not suicidal, Paul, don't worry. I am pretty tough.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Does being tough mean you have to suffer through things like this alone?

context.speaker: client
context.text: I just felt like the bed was safe and the living room was scary.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: So you took to bed like your mother did.

therapist_turn: So you took to bed like your mother did.
client_response: She had post-partum. What's my excuse... post-non-partum?
internal:
[Perception] He was making it sound like I was doing some neat little family-repeat thing, like I just folded into bed because my mother did. And maybe that’s true in the shallowest sense, but what I wanted him to see is that this wasn’t me being dramatic or lazy or “needing attention.” The bed felt safe because everything else felt exposed and wrong. The living room, the normal parts of the house, the parts where I’m supposed to be functioning, talking, being a person—those felt like a place where I’d have to pretend I was okay. And I wasn’t okay. Not after the loss, not with my own body feeling like it had betrayed me, and definitely not with the way he kept linking me to my mother like that was the whole story.

[Decision] So I answered sarcastically, because if I said it straight out I might have had to admit how much it hurt. I wanted to push back on being lumped in with her. She had her own thing, and I have mine. I’m not using this as an excuse. I hate needing this much help. But I also can’t keep pretending there’s some clean, respectable explanation for why I can’t just get up and be fine. “Post-non-partum” was me saying: there’s no script for this, no acceptable label, and I’m angry that I’m being expected to act like there is.

internal:
[Perception] He’s doing that thing again—turning it into “you want to keep me around” and making it sound like I’m attached in some needy, obvious way. And underneath that, he’s still circling the same ugly question: that it’s not just me being “an angry person,” that there’s something about my father in here, something I’m supposed to admit. That feels too exposed. Too much like being pinned down and interpreted instead of just being heard. I can feel the old panic of, here we go, now he’s going to make this about my deepest stuff again, and I don’t want to open that door.

[Decision] So I’m going to put the brakes on it by making it light, sharp, and a little ridiculous. If I act like this is about liking him as a person, and joke about the rules and the “Laura” thing, I can keep the conversation on the surface where I still have control. I’m not giving him the part that hurts. I’m not letting him get too close to the thing I can’t afford to have named. I can stay friendly, even charming, but I’m not handing over my vulnerability or letting him make me feel trapped in his interpretation.

context.text: I just remembered a dream I had this week. Mr. Donaldson called me in for a meeting. Only it wasn't in an office. It was... It was in an old garage. context.speaker: client
context.text: You know, Walter and April, they both think that the world is supposed to be on their shoulders, and they're both incapable of receiving support. One's stopping therapy, the other wants more sessions.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: So you're going to continue.

therapist_turn: So you're going to continue.
client_response: You know what I realized this week? Practicing this way, I may never know whether I help people or not. It's not like I'm trying to get them to pass their driving test or do better on their SATs or something. The only measure I have of whether I'm helping somebody or not is how my patients feel about it and how their lives go on from there. And they won't know that until long after we've stopped therapy.
internal:
[Perception] The therapist’s “So you’re going to continue” landed like a test of whether I was actually announcing a change or just circling around one. It connected directly to the part of me that’s unsettled by the fact that I may never get clean feedback about whether I’m helpful. Walter and April are a perfect example: one leaves, one asks for more, and neither outcome actually tells me if I’m doing something right. That’s the puzzle I’m stuck on — if the only evidence is their subjective experience and the long, delayed effects of their life after therapy, then what am I supposed to use as a real measure? And if I can’t measure it, am I just supposed to accept permanent uncertainty as part of the job?

[Decision] I decided not to hide behind the usual “I’m just here to walk with people” stance, at least not in this moment. I want to keep thinking about whether there’s a more solid way to understand my impact without turning myself into a fixer or abandoning the humility I value. So I’m staying with the uncertainty instead of resolving it too quickly, because the question matters: if I can never know directly whether I help, then I need to figure out what kind of knowing is actually possible in this work.

That was my way of trying to make the ending less absolute, less like a death. And then I turned to her appearance, her dress, and asked if she had a date tonight because that was safer than saying, plainly, that I was watching her leave me and trying to understand how she could still have a life that moved on without me in it. What I wanted her to see was that I was circling the real subject: this is ending, but not cleanly, and I’m trying to locate myself in it.
